name: Sumerian city-states
summary: In the marshy south of Mesopotamia, Uruk and its neighbours grew into the world's first cities and, by c. 3300 BCE, the first writing. Through the Early Dynastic period (c. 2900–2334 BCE) rival city-states such as Kish, Ur, Lagash and Umma fought over land and water, until Lugalzagesi united Sumer, only to lose it to Sargon of Akkad. All dates are approximate (middle chronology).

Earliest unequivocal written documents (proto-cuneiform) appear at Uruk
Jemdet Nasr period: writing becomes more abstract; cities run central administrations

Era of Gilgamesh of Uruk and Enmebaragesi of Kish, kings of later legend

Early Dynastic I–II: Kish and Uruk (Enmebaragesi, Gilgamesh)
Dynasty of Ur-Nanshe at Lagash (Eannatum, Entemena, Urukagina)

name: Akkadian Empire
summary: Sargon of Akkad (r. c. 2334–2279 BCE) conquered Sumer and campaigned from the Gulf to Syria and Elam, creating the first empire to rule all Mesopotamia. His grandson Naram-Sin crushed a great revolt and took the realm to its widest extent, but after Shar-kali-sharri (d. c. 2193 BCE) the state broke apart under Gutian and Amorite pressure and fell c. 2154 BCE. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Sargon comes to power and founds a dynasty ruling from Akkad (site still unknown)
Sargon defeats Lugalzagesi in three battles, razes Uruk's walls and takes Sumer
Sargon takes Mari and claims the 'Upper Country' to the Cedar Forest
Sargon dies; Rimush reconquers rebel cities including Ur, Umma and Lagash
Manishtushu leads a fleet down the Gulf against 32 kings; takes Anshan

Reign of Shu-turul ends; Akkad's empire is gone as Gutians dominate

name: Third Dynasty of Ur (Neo-Sumerian Empire)
summary: After the Gutian interlude, Ur-Nammu of Ur (r. c. 2112–2094 BCE) reunited Sumer and Akkad, and his son Shulgi built a centralised, bureaucratic state of some twenty provinces ringed by a military periphery along the Zagros. Amorite incursions, revolts and the breakaway of Isin weakened his successors, and c. 2004 BCE an Elamite coalition sacked Ur. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Ur-Nammu takes power at Ur and founds the Third Dynasty
Ur-Nammu dies in battle in the eastern highlands; Shulgi begins a 48-year reign
Shulgi, a god by his 21st year, reforms weights, taxes and the bureaucracy

name: Old Babylonian Empire (Hammurabi)
summary: Hammurabi (r. c. 1792–1750 BCE) turned Babylon from one Amorite kingdom among many into the master of Mesopotamia, conquering Larsa, Mari and Eshnunna and issuing his famous law code. Under his son Samsu-iluna revolts wrecked the southern cities and the far south broke away as the Sealand dynasty; a shrunken kingdom lasted until the Hittite king Mursili I sacked Babylon c. 1595 BCE. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Hammurabi succeeds Sin-muballit as king of Babylon
Hammurabi conquers Larsa and annexes Rim-Sin's kingdom in the south
Hammurabi takes Mari on the Euphrates; its palace is destroyed by 1759

name: Hittite Empire
summary: From their capital Hattusa in central Anatolia, the Hittite kings Hattusili I and Mursili I raided as far as Aleppo and Babylon (c. 1595 BCE) before the Old Kingdom sank into court strife. Suppiluliuma I (c. 1350–1322 BCE) broke Mitanni and made the Hittites masters of Syria; his successors fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh and made peace. Around 1190 BCE, amid the wider Bronze Age collapse, Hattusa was abandoned and the empire vanished. All dates are approximate (middle chronology).

Telipinu's reign closes the Old Kingdom after years of internal strife

name: Egypt's New Kingdom empire
summary: Ahmose I expelled the Hyksos and reunited Egypt (c. 1549–1524 BCE); his successors, above all Thutmose III, built an empire from Nubia beyond the Fourth Cataract to the Euphrates. Egypt contested Syria with Mitanni and then the Hittites until the treaty of c. 1259 BCE, but after Ramesses III fought off the Sea Peoples its power ebbed, and by Ramesses XI's death in 1077 BCE the country was split between Tanis and Thebes. Reign dates follow the conventional low chronology and are approximate.

name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
summary: From 911 BCE Assyrian kings reconquered northern Mesopotamia, and Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III made Assyria the dominant power of the Near East. After a long spell of weak kings, Tiglath-Pileser III (745–727 BCE) more than doubled the empire, and the Sargonid kings took Israel, Babylon and, in 671 BCE, Egypt. Within two decades of Ashurbanipal's death the Babylonians and Medes destroyed Assur (614), Nineveh (612) and the last Assyrian army at Harran (609).

name: Neo-Babylonian Empire (Nebuchadnezzar II)
summary: Nabopolassar threw off Assyrian rule in 626 BCE and, allied with the Medes, destroyed Assyria by 609 BCE. His son Nebuchadnezzar II (605–562 BCE) won Syria and the Levant at Carchemish, destroyed Jerusalem in 587 BCE and rebuilt Babylon in splendour. After his death three short reigns ended in Nabonidus, whose long absence in Arabia left Babylon exposed; Cyrus of Persia took the city in 539 BCE.

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
summary: Cyrus the Great overthrew the Medes in 550 BCE and took Lydia and Babylon; Cambyses added Egypt and Darius I pushed the frontier to the Indus and into Europe, ruling c. 5.5 million km², the largest empire yet seen. Defeats in Greece (490, 480–479 BCE) and the loss of Egypt (404–343 BCE) dented but did not break it; Alexander of Macedon destroyed it in 334–330 BCE.

name: Roman Republic and Empire
summary: The Roman Republic (from c. 509 BCE) conquered Italy, then defeated Carthage and the Hellenistic kingdoms to dominate the Mediterranean, before civil wars ended in one-man rule under Augustus (27 BCE). The Empire peaked under Trajan at about 5 million km² (117 CE), survived the crisis of the third century, and was split for good between East and West in 395. The Western half lost its provinces to Germanic peoples and ended when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476.

name: Empire of Alexander the Great
summary: Philip II (359–336 BCE) made Macedon the master of Greece; his son Alexander III conquered the whole Persian Empire and pushed on to the Indus before dying in Babylon in 323 BCE. His generals kept the empire nominally united under his half-brother and infant son, but after both were murdered they took royal titles, and the battle of Ipsus (301 BCE) fixed its partition into rival kingdoms.

name: Maurya Empire
summary: Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nanda dynasty of Magadha c. 321 BCE and, after war with Seleucus I, won the lands up to the Hindu Kush. Bindusara pushed into the Deccan and Ashoka conquered Kalinga c. 261 BCE, ruling nearly all of South Asia except the far south before turning to Buddhism. After Ashoka's death in 232 BCE weaker kings followed, and the general Pushyamitra Shunga killed the last, Brihadratha, c. 185 BCE.

name: Seleucid Empire
summary: Seleucus I took Babylon in 312 BCE and, after Ipsus and Corupedium, ruled from the Aegean to the borders of India. Bactria and Parthia broke away in the mid-3rd century; Antiochus III restored much of the realm but lost Anatolia to Rome after Magnesia (190 BCE), and the Parthians took Mesopotamia in 141 BCE. Reduced to Syria and torn by dynastic wars, the kingdom was annexed by Pompey in 63 BCE.

name: Ptolemaic Kingdom
summary: Ptolemy I, Alexander's satrap in Egypt from 323 BCE, made himself king in 305 BCE and added Cyrenaica, Cyprus and Coele-Syria; under Ptolemy III in the 240s the kingdom reached its height, campaigning as far as Babylonia. Native revolts, the loss of Coele-Syria (200 BCE) and dynastic feuds weakened it as Rome's influence grew; Cleopatra VII's defeat at Actium led to Egypt's annexation by Rome in 30 BCE.

name: Parthian Empire
summary: Arsaces I, leader of the Parni, founded the Arsacid state in Parthia c. 247 BCE; Mithridates I (c. 171–132 BCE) took Media and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids, and Mithridates II extended Parthian power from the Euphrates to Afghanistan. Astride the Silk Road, Parthia fought Rome for three centuries, destroying Crassus at Carrhae but losing Ctesiphon to Trajan, Avidius Cassius and Severus. Weakened by civil war, the last king, Artabanus IV, fell to Ardashir I of Persis in 224 CE.

name: Qin and Han China
summary: The state of Qin conquered its last rivals in 221 BCE and its king became the First Emperor, standardising script, coinage and law, but the dynasty collapsed in revolts soon after his death and ended in 206 BCE. Liu Bang founded the Han in 202 BCE; under Emperor Wu (141–87 BCE) it drove back the Xiongnu and expanded into Central Asia, Korea and the far south. After Wang Mang's Xin interlude (9–23 CE) the Eastern Han ruled from Luoyang until rebellion and warlords ended it in 220 CE.

name: Xiongnu
summary: Modu Chanyu (209–174 BCE) united the nomads of the Mongolian Plateau into a confederation that humbled the early Han and drove the Yuezhi west. Emperor Wu's wars from 133 BCE broke Xiongnu power; a succession war ended with Huhanye submitting to Han, and in 48 CE the confederation split into Southern and Northern Xiongnu. Han campaigns in 89–91 CE destroyed the Northern state, whose chanyu fled west.

name: Kushan Empire
summary: Kujula Kadphises united the Yuezhi tribes of Bactria in the 1st century CE, and his successors pushed into north-western India. Under Kanishka I (c. 127–150) the empire stretched from Central Asia to the Ganges plain, ruled from Purushapura and Mathura and linking the Silk Road, India and Rome. After Vasudeva I (d. c. 225) Sasanian Persia took the west, and the eastern 'Little Kushans' faded under Gupta suzerainty and the Kidarites by c. 375.

name: Sasanian Empire
summary: Ardashir I overthrew the Parthians in 224 and his son Shapur I humiliated Rome, capturing the emperor Valerian in 260. For four centuries the Sasanians rivalled Rome and Byzantium; Khosrow I (531–579) sacked Antioch and took Yemen, and Khosrow II briefly held the Levant and Egypt. Exhausted by the war of 602–628 and the civil war that followed, the empire fell to the Arab conquests, ending with Yazdegerd III's death in 651.

name: Gupta Empire
summary: From the Gangetic plain, Chandragupta I (c. 319–335) raised the Gupta dynasty to imperial rank; Samudragupta's conquests and Chandragupta II's defeat of the Western Satraps made it the dominant power of northern India, a 'Golden Age' of art and science. Skandagupta repelled the Huns c. 455, but after him the empire lost ground to feudatories and to the Alchon Huns under Toramana and Mihirakula, and it had faded by the mid-6th century.
